Zero
ZEE-roh
n.
Italian zero, from Medieval Latin zephirum, from Arabic sifr (cipher, emptiness) — itself a translation of Sanskrit shūnya (void, empty). Zero as a numerical symbol entered European mathematics via Arab transmission of Hindu arithmetic in the ninth–thirteenth centuries; it is absent from Hebrew, Greek, and Roman numeral systems and therefore from the biblical text as a written digit.

Biblical Definition

The number zero, as a written digit or place-holder, did not exist in the numeral systems used by the biblical authors. Hebrew, Greek, and Roman numeration all begin at one; the concept of an empty position was supplied by Arabic-Hindu mathematics a millennium after the New Testament was complete. Yet the reality zero encodes — absolute nothingness before the act of God — saturates the biblical worldview. The foundational text is Genesis 1:2: the earth was tohu wabohu, formless and empty, darkness over the face of the deep — a state of radical incompleteness prior to God’s creative word. Isaiah drives it further: all nations before God are “as nothing,” counted by Him as “less than nothing, and” (Isa 40:17) — the creature, stripped of divine sustenance, reduced to ontological zero. The Incarnation itself enacts a voluntary descent toward creaturely emptiness: the Son “emptied Himself” (heauton ekenosen, Phil 2:7), taking the form of a bondservant in the kenosis. Zero as a theological concept is therefore not the denial of existence but the confession that all existence depends moment by moment on the God who speaks being out of nothing (ex nihilo) and who alone is self-existent and non-derivative. To stand before God as zero is not annihilation but the beginning of worship.

Origin & Era

Zero: the arithmetical symbol for nothing; a concept absent from biblical numeral systems as a written digit, but whose theological substance — the absolute nothingness of the creature apart from God, and the ex nihilo foundation of creation — is everywhere in Scripture.

expand to see more

ZERO, n. The arithmetical symbol 0, representing the absence of quantity. Introduced into European mathematics from Arabic-Hindu sources in the medieval period; not present in the Hebrew, Greek, or Roman systems used by the scriptural authors.

Theologically, zero names the ontological status of every created thing apart from the sustaining will of God. The Creator alone is self-existent (aseity); every creature is derivative. To confess this is not nihilism but creaturely humility — the recognition that all being, all goodness, and all intelligibility flows from the One who spoke the world from nothing.

Key Scripture

Genesis 1:2 — "And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters."

Isaiah 40:17 — "All nations before him are as nothing; and they are counted to him less than nothing, and vanity."

Philippians 2:7 — "But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:"

Psalm 139:8 — "If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there."

Modern Corruption

Secular philosophy converts the biblical ex nihilo (creation from nothing) into atheistic nihilism (nothing at the ground of all things), turning the creature’s absolute dependence on God into the claim that there is no God and therefore nothing ultimately matters.

expand to see more

Nihilism in its modern form (Nietzsche, existentialism, postmodernism) begins where biblical theology ends: the creature is nothing without God. But it draws the opposite conclusion — if the creature is nothing, then nothing is. It mistakes the creature’s derivative nothingness (real existence sustained from outside itself) for absolute nothingness (no existence at all). The result is the counsel of despair: if life has no transcendent foundation, it has no meaning. Scripture reverses the conclusion entirely: the creature’s nothingness before God is the ground of its dignity, for it exists only because the infinitely good God willed it into being and sustains it every moment.

Eastern religious philosophies (Buddhism’s sunyata, Hindu nirvana) treat the zero-state as the goal: absorption into undifferentiated nothingness, the dissolution of the self. Scripture knows no such doctrine of dissolution. The redeemed stand before the throne as distinct persons, glorified and numbered among the great multitude that no one could count (Rev 7:9). God does not create persons to unmake them; He creates them to glorify Himself forever.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Zero entered the Western mind through Arabic mathematics from the Sanskrit shūnya (void) — a concept the biblical authors encoded not in a digit but in the language of formlessness, emptiness, and the absolute creative power of God over the void.

expand to see more

Sanskrit shūnya — void, empty; the original mathematical concept of a place-holder.

Arabic sifr — cipher, emptiness; gave English both “zero” and “cipher.”

Medieval Latin zephirum — zero; the Latinized form that passed into Italian and then English.

Hebrew tohu — formlessness, wasteness (Gen 1:2); the biblical parallel to zero as pre-creational void.

Greek kenos — empty; root of kenosis (Phil 2:7), the voluntary self-emptying of Christ in the Incarnation.

Usage

"The tohu wabohu of Genesis 1:2 is not absolute nothingness but the theological zero-state: a world without form or filling, awaiting the creative word of God."

"Every creature before God is ontological zero — derivative, sustained, dependent — which is not a humiliation but a creaturely dignity: we exist because He willed it and wills it still."

"The kenosis of Philippians 2:7 does not mean the Son ceased to be divine but that He voluntarily took on the limitations of creaturely form — the Infinite willingly entering the near-zero of human finitude for our redemption."
